They gave me a thousand words and told me to write whatever comes to mind. First comes the refrigerator's hum, unnoticed until now. It sounds like a distant motorboat, or maybe a bee trapped in a jar. I am supposed to be spontaneous, but spontaneity is a trick: the moment you try to be spontaneous, you become a performer. Still, I will try now. I will write without stopping, without editing, without looking back. That is the only rule. So here I am, typing fast, hoping the words arrive before the doubt does. One sentence at a time, then another.

I remember a summer evening when I was eight, chasing fireflies in a neighbor's field. The air smelled of cut grass and gasoline from a distant lawnmower. I caught one firefly in a jar and watched its light pulse against the glass. I thought it was a tiny star that had fallen and needed saving. My father told me to let it go before it died of fright. I opened the lid, and the firefly flew out, blinking once as if to say goodbye. That was my first lesson in holding things loosely. I still think about that small light.

Writing this feels like picking a lock with a hairpin. I keep fumbling for the right words, and they keep slipping out of reach. There is a certain kind of pressure that comes from a limit. A thousand words is not a lot, but it is enough to build a small room. So I will build a room here, with one window and a chair. The chair is empty, but you can sit in it if you like. I will leave the window open a crack so the air can move through. That way, the words will not go stale.

I have been thinking about the word "enough." It is a small word, but it carries a lot. When do you know when something is enough? A thousand words is an arbitrary boundary, like a fence around a field. The field does not end at the fence; it just stops being yours. I am trying to make these words yours. I want you to walk into this room and feel that the window is open, that the chair is steady, that the floor does not creak too much. I want you to stay for a while, but not too long.

My grandmother told a story about a woman who collected rain. The woman had a hundred jars lined up on her porch, and every time it rained, she would run outside and fill them one by one. When the drought came, she had enough water to share with the whole town. I asked

The last time I counted to a thousand, I was seven years old and lying on a quilt in the backyard. My grandmother had told me that if I could count to one thousand without losing my place, I would earn a quarter, which at that age felt like the kind of wealth that could buy five candy bars or a small plastic horse from the dime store. So I lay there with the grass pressing against my back and the sky turning the color of peach skin, and I counted. One, two, three. Somewhere around four hundred and twelve, a dog barked, and I forgot whether the next number was four hundred thirteen or five hundred thirteen. I stopped and started over three times. By the time I reached one thousand, the stars had come out, and my grandmother had fallen asleep in the lawn chair beside me. She never paid me the quarter, but I didn't care. I had touched the edge of a very large number, and the number had touched me back.

This is different. You have given me one thousand words, not numbers, and the words are supposed to come from me without a plan. But writing without a plan is like counting without a flashlight: you know the path is there, but you cannot see the next stone. I am not seven anymore. I am sitting in a room that is too warm, and the light from the screen makes my eyes feel dry. There is a cup of tea to my left. It has gone cold. I keep thinking I should drink it, but I don't. Cold tea is not sad, exactly, but it is a kind of small failure.

Maybe I should tell you about the day I realized that words have weight. I was in high school, and my English teacher wrote a sentence on the board: "The house was empty." She asked us what it meant. Someone said, "Nobody was home." She said, "No, it means somebody used to live there." That was the first time I understood that absence is a presence. The empty house is full of missing. The cold tea is full of the moment when it was hot, and I was too busy to notice. Every word I write here is a room, and you are walking through it, and I am somewhere behind the drywall, knocking.

I could write about the man I saw on the bus yesterday. He was carrying a cardboard box with a handle made of duct tape. The box had a label on the side that said "fragile" in red marker, but the word was misspelled as "fragil." He held it on his lap with both arms wrapped around it, the way you hold a sleeping child. Every time the bus lurched, he tightened his grip. I wondered what was inside. Maybe it was dishes, or a clock, or the ashes of a dog. Maybe it was nothing at all, and he was just practicing holding something carefully. I wanted to ask him, but the bus was crowded and I was afraid of what he might say. So I watched him from the corner of my eye and made up stories. In one story, the box contained a set of hand-painted teacups from a mother who had died. In another, it held a collection of rocks from every beach he had ever walked on. In the best story, the box held a single photograph of a woman laughing, and he was taking it to her, and when he arrived she would open it and the laugh would spill out like light.

But that is not true. I made it up. That is what I do. I make up things and hope they feel true. Maybe that is the only honesty I have.

Now I am at a wall. I have written many words, but I do not know how many. I could count them, but counting words is like counting breaths: the moment you notice, the rhythm changes. I am not supposed to stop. The instruction says one thousand words, and I am giving you whatever comes to me. Here is what comes: I am thinking about my grandmother's hands. She used to peel apples in one long spiral, the skin coming away like a ribbon. She said if the ribbon broke, you would have bad luck for a day. I would stand beside her at the kitchen sink, watching the green stripe curl away from the white fruit, and I would hold my breath until she finished. She never broke the ribbon. Not once. I think about that now as a kind of magic, but also as a kind of patience. She had learned to let the knife do the work, to trust the curve of the apple and the sharpness of the blade. Writing is like that, too. You have to let the words do the work, to trust the curve of the sentence. I am trying to trust.

There is a fly in the room now. It is buzzing against the window, throwing its small body against the glass. I want to open the window, but it is cold outside, and the tea is already cold. The fly will die soon. They only live about a month. I do not know why that makes me sad. It is just a fly. But it is so convinced that the window is the way out, and the real way out is three inches to the left. I want to tell it, "The opening is right there. You are so close." But I can't speak fly, and it can't hear me. Maybe that is how God feels, or the universe, or whatever you want to call the thing that watches us bang against our own glass.

I am running out of things to say, which is strange because I have not run out of words. There are always more words. The dictionary has hundreds of thousands of them. The problem is that they start to feel like coins from a foreign country: I can hold them in my hand, but I cannot spend them here. I could list them. I could write "velvet," "harbor," "lantern," "quiet." I could write "the moon is a comma in a long sentence." I could write "I am sorry for the cold tea, and for the fly, and for the man on the bus whose story I invented." I could write "I am trying to be honest without being seen." That is the hardest trick, I think, to be seen without being seen. To write yourself onto a page and then step back, like a painter stepping away from the canvas, hoping the image holds.

I am at the point now where the words are no longer flowing. They are dripping. I am squeezing them out one by one like water from a stone. But that is okay. The last time I counted to a thousand, the numbers also became thick and heavy around seven hundred. I wanted to quit. I wanted to stand up, run inside, watch cartoons. But I didn't. I lay there and I finished, and when I said "one thousand" to the darkening sky, my grandmother was asleep, and I was alone with the number, and it was enough. So maybe this is enough. Maybe you are not asleep. Maybe you are reading this and wondering if I will make it to the end. I will. I am at the end now. I can feel it.

Para5: My grandmother told a story about a woman who collected rain. The woman had a hundred jars lined up on her porch, and every time it rained, she would run outside and fill them one by one. When the drought came, she had enough water to share with the whole town. I asked my grandmother why the woman did not just save the rain for herself. She said, "Because water is only good when it moves. Still water is just waiting." I still think about that when I write. Words are like water. They are only good when they move.

Para6: I am halfway now, or a little past. The room I built still stands; the window is open, the chair empty. I keep looking at it, expecting someone to sit down. Maybe you are sitting there now, reading this and wondering why I am so preoccupied with rooms and windows and water. I have no good answer. These are just the things that come when you ask for a thousand words. The mind is a strange attic. You reach in, and you pull out a jar of rain, a firefly, even a grandmother's story. You never know what is there.

Para7: Let me tell you about this morning's sky. It was a pale blue, almost white at the edges, as if the night had been rinsed out and hung to dry. I stood at the window with my coffee and watched a bird land on the telephone wire. The bird did not sing. It just sat there, adjusting its wings, looking around. I thought, that bird is not worried about word counts or room metaphors. It is just alive, and that is enough. Then it flew away, and I was alone with the pale sky and the quiet. I remember clearly.

Para8: Every piece of writing has a moment when you realize you are no longer in control. The words have taken the wheel. I am there now. I am not choosing these sentences; they are choosing me. It feels like falling through a net that you wove yourself. You trust the threads hold, but you are not sure. That is the only way to write anything true. You have to let the net catch you. You have to believe that the words will be there when you reach for them, even when they feel like rain slipping through all your fingers.

Para9: I am nearly done. Nine hundred words have passed through me, and I have not stopped to count them until now. That is a small victory. The room I built is still standing. The window is still open. The chair is still empty, but maybe that is okay. An empty chair is not a failure; it is an invitation. So consider this your invitation. Sit down. Look out the window. There is a bird on the wire, and the sky is pale, and somewhere a jar of rain is waiting to be shared. This is what I meant to say.
